An agreed payment pause gives cash relief now: chart the debt and the repayments that follow

Use five charts to separate skipped cash payments, outstanding principal and deferred interest, then compare a later payoff with a higher resumed payment.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Trace a hypothetical agreed payment pause and two repayment paths

Interactive planning lab

Payments not paid during the agreed pause$2,713.64
Resumed monthly payment to restore the original payoff month$1,096.24
Extra total interest if the original payment resumes$344.76

Original hypothetical instalment-loan illustration, not a lender quote or a Canadian mortgage calculator. Six month-end payments are made before the agreed pause begins in month 7. Interest each month equals outstanding original principal times the entered nominal annual rate divided by 12. During the pause, no cash is paid and interest is recorded separately. No interest is ever charged on that deferred-interest balance, during or after the pause. Once payments resume, they pay current interest first, then deferred interest, then original principal. One path resumes the original payment; another solves a higher payment to clear both balances by the original final month. The final payment is limited to the amount owed. All payments are assumed affordable and made when due. The agreement, allocation rule and continuing exemption from interest on deferred interest are model assumptions, not a statement that every relief arrangement uses them. There are no fees, rate changes, insurance, property taxes, rounding to cents, tax effects, eligibility tests, credit-reporting results or household savings returns. Lower payments during the pause are temporary cash relief, not income or debt forgiveness.

The central idea

Not paying an instalment today does not mean that debt has been forgiven. The agreement’s interest treatment and repayment calendar determine what remains due.

01

Start with an agreed change to the payment calendar

A temporary payment pause can free cash for immediate household needs. It also changes when a lender receives principal and interest. An agreed change to the contract is different from simply missing a payment.

FCAC’s personal-loan guidance explains that a loan combines the amount borrowed, interest, fees and regular repayments. It notes that renegotiating terms may help when circumstances change and directs borrowers having payment difficulties to their lender.

The tool constructs one possible agreement. It does not establish access to a payment holiday, lender approval or credit-reporting treatment. No actual product terms or Canadian mortgage payment convention are reproduced.

02

Write down exactly which balance earns interest

The starting example is a CAD 20,000 loan with 24 monthly payments and an invented 8% nominal annual rate divided by twelve for monthly interest. Its unrounded monthly payment is about CAD 904.55. After six payments, the remaining original principal is about CAD 15,294.91.

The agreed pause covers months 7, 8 and 9. No payment is made in those months. Interest continues to accrue on the unchanged original principal at about CAD 101.97 per month. The deferred-interest ledger reaches about CAD 305.90, making total debt about CAD 15,600.81 at the end of month 9.

The constructed agreement never charges interest on that deferred-interest ledger, either during or after the pause. It keeps the original principal and unpaid interest separate. Actual agreements can define different treatment, repayment allocation and relief periods.

For Canadian mortgage context, FCAC’s deferral guidance explicitly states an expectation that federally regulated institutions not charge interest on deferred interest. That mortgage-specific context is one reason not to assume a payment pause automatically means compounding all unpaid interest into an interest-bearing balance. This generic model is not an assessment of a particular mortgage relief measure.

03

Count the payments not made without treating them as a new grant

The three paused payments free about CAD 2,713.64 of cash compared with the original calendar. That may help fund bills during an interruption. The model does not assume this cash is saved, invested or sufficient for the household’s needs.

The same amount is not added wholesale to the loan. The principal that would have been repaid was already included in the CAD 15,294.91 outstanding before the pause. Adding the full skipped instalments again would count some principal twice.

The waterfall starts with that outstanding original principal and adds only newly deferred interest. It reconciles the actual modeled obligation at the pause’s end. Cash relief, extra debt relative to a no-pause path and new interest charges are related amounts with different definitions.

04

Resume the original payment and allow the payoff date to move

In the first repayment path, the monthly payment returns to about CAD 904.55 in month 10. Each payment first covers current interest on the remaining original principal, then repays deferred interest, then reduces original principal. Deferred interest itself still earns no interest.

Under the default assumptions, the loan finishes in month 28 rather than month 24. The last payment is limited to the amount still owed. Total interest is about CAD 2,053.86, compared with CAD 1,709.10 without a pause: an increase of about CAD 344.76.

Even without interest on deferred interest, principal remains outstanding for longer. Interest continues on that principal. A three-payment pause therefore need not move the payoff date by exactly three months when the original payment resumes.

05

Restore the original final month with a larger resumed payment

The other repayment path clears both ledgers by the original month 24. It uses the same allocation rule and pause but solves for a resumed payment of about CAD 1,096.24 from month 10 onward.

Total interest is about CAD 1,870.89 in this default path. That exceeds the no-pause interest by about CAD 161.79 and is lower than in the original-payment path. The higher later payment is the price of restoring the earlier payoff date under these terms; the calculation does not establish that the household can afford it.

The total-repayment bars include original principal and all interest charged through each path’s own payoff date. They do not discount future payments or attach a value to the immediate cash relief. A cost comparison alone cannot decide whether the pause resolves a household’s financial difficulty.

06

Put the revised agreement beside a household cash budget

Check the actual pause dates, interest-bearing balances, allocation of later payments, fees, resumed amount and final payoff date. If a rule exempts deferred interest from further interest only temporarily, a model assuming a continuing exemption needs to be changed.

FCAC’s mortgage-difficulty guidance describes the importance of information about revised costs, payments and amortization before accepting relief. Its expectations concern the stated mortgage circumstances; this loan illustration does not determine whether those circumstances apply.

Build the household cash calendar using the agreed payments and independently verified receipts. Identify what supports the resumed payment after the pause. The matrix shows how the modeled interest cost changes with rate and pause length, while leaving approval, future income and affordability unresolved.
